A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Cardiverse and retain identifiable methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary sections support reliable comparison, including material relocated between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original game-design, code-generation, and gameplay-AI evaluations, plus component ablations, in Sections 4 and 8.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds human ratings, consistency-metric validation, heuristic-opponent comparisons, and policy-pool sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The graph-based variation pipeline, gameplay-record code validation, and self-play-selected heuristic ensemble remain substantively the same. v2 expands implementation details and replaces Q-function terminology with heuristic functions. The strategy, metric, and refinement prompts already appear in v1 Section 9; their fuller explanation does not establish a new algorithm.

E1.justification: The original 106-game collection and principal evaluation sets remain. v2 adds human evaluation of Go Fish variants, gameplay comparisons on Leduc Hold'em and Uno, and consistency-evaluation scenarios using deliberately mismatched game descriptions. These introduce substantive new evaluation tasks and conditions beyond the retained benchmarks.

E2.justification: The existing novelty baselines, code-generation ablations, and CoT, ReAct, Reflexion, and Belief agents remain. Appendix C.1 newly evaluates human-designed RLCard heuristics on two games, adding a limited non-LLM comparison outside the retained main gameplay benchmark.

E3.justification: New protocols include five-point ratings of nine summaries per participant, consistency checks using five verified games with five records each and descriptions at 95% or 70% embedding similarity, gameplay comparisons across player orderings, and a policy-population sweep over n=2, 4, and 6. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v1 already contains ensemble and optimization ablations. v2 adds controlled validation of the PCon judge in Appendix B.4, policy-population sensitivity in C.3, and further graph and generated-game case studies in Appendix A. These address metric validity, parameter sensitivity, and qualitative behavior beyond the original analyses.

E5.justification: Beyond the retained means, standard deviations, and paired t-tests, v2 introduces mixed-effects estimates with standard errors, z-tests, and confidence intervals for human ratings, chi-square tests for heuristic comparisons, and standard-error shading for PCon. It also newly discloses 50 runs per game for ablations; this does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain their point estimates, but gameplay and ablation entries change. For example, Table 3 changes the proposed method's varied-game advantage from 12.5±24.8 to 19.7±30.5 while retaining its overall 16.3±22.6. v2 also adds human-rating, PCon-validation, heuristic-comparison, and sensitivity results. The revised existing scores are not explained as an algorithmic improvement.

T1.justification: The policy-averaging, QMS, and win-advantage equations remain mathematically equivalent, with no new proofs. The new limitations discussion adds a brief complexity comparison: O(n^3) for the clustering implementation versus a proposed O(n) Gaussian-mixture alternative.

C1.justification: Both versions claim the same three contributions: graph-supported novel mechanics, gameplay-validated code generation, and scalable gameplay AI without per-decision LLM calls. The emphasis on game variations clarifies the mutation-based task already described in v1; the additional evaluations support rather than redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 retains earlier caveats about mechanic conflicts, validation cost, and missing opponent-intention modeling. It adds substantive boundaries concerning small controlled variations, detailed human inputs, scaling to other genres, clustering cost, weaker-model code generation, and embedding-metric precision. It also interprets the new sensitivity plateau and subjective design evaluations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and identifies the card-description source. It newly specifies UPGMA clustering, n=4 policy generation, 400 games per selection evaluation, three code-generation attempts, explicit sampling defaults, and five-turn baseline histories. These materially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to the previously used implementation.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially repositions the work within P-creativity and existing mechanic-recombination research, replacing v1's stronger assertions about missing hierarchical representations. Genuine additions include Conceptual Game Expansion, Chaos Cards, Mechanic Maker, and broader LLM design research. The Large Concept Models connection is removed; publication updates to retained references are not new works.

P1.justification: The introduction, mechanics-related work, and gameplay-AI explanation are substantially rewritten. Code-generation details move into Appendix B, limitations receive a dedicated main-text section, and supplementary material is reorganized into Appendices A–E with a contents list. Terminology changes accompany this broader narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overall pipeline figure, merges and redraws the mechanics diagrams, and redraws the gameplay-AI and code-generation workflows. Table 2 becomes separate common/varied panels, and new study tables and a PCon plot appear. Existing embedding panels and gameplay radar plots are relocated, while additional explicit mechanic graphs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on embedding similarity for design evaluation and unvalidated LLM consistency scores through human ratings and controlled PCon checks. Additional AI analyses, clearer implementation details, and better-qualified positioning strengthen support and reproducibility. The user study remains limited to Go Fish summaries, and duplicated matchup labels in Table 6 plus unexplained score revisions weaken reporting clarity, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.
